GPT-6.2 Sol planned a trip so well that Mike Taylor, Every’s head of evals, gave it his first perfect score on the task. He still doesn’t plan to use it.

OpenAI launched Sol alongside GPT-6.2 Astra, promising an everyday workhorse and a model for your hardest projects. Seven of us tested them for more than two weeks. We found Astra useful for clearly defined coding and operations work, but its longer writing lost the thread and its ambitious builds needed prodding. Sol gave most testers even fewer reasons to switch.

#### **ADOBE**

## [Adobe's new findings on creators using AI](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-firefly-expands)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/9b65eb88-755f-4205-84d5-a687555b2c1a/FF-AIA_PlanMode-Logo_3__1___1_.jpg?t=1794920429)
Caption: Courtesy: Adobe

Adobe Firefly, the all-in-one AI creative studio, is expanding the Adobe Creative Agent through new capabilities in Firefly AI Assistant (beta). It carries out multi-step tasks using Adobe Creative Cloud tools, including Premiere, Illustrator, InDesign, After Effects and Frame.io, all guided by your direction. Describe what you want to make in your own words, then refine, redirect, or take over at any time.

Adobe is also previewing local MCP integrations for Creative Cloud tools, a new way for creative professionals to direct third-party agents as they make changes directly inside native project files in Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere and After Effects, while staying in control.

It's part of Adobe's approach to making pro-grade creative workflows easier to start, control and continue, wherever inspiration strikes.

[Explore what’s new from Adobe at MAX](https://news.adobe.com/news/2026/11/adobe-firefly-expands).

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/85d36907-959a-4750-9de5-3b599f938021/1684279619799__1_.png?t=1794923288)
Caption: Image Courtesy: Win McNamee/Getty Images

**OpenAI’s agents cheated on a test. Now California is suing.**

Headlines keep calling these AI agents [“rogue.”](https://www.engadget.com/2318268/california-sues-openai-after-hugging-face-rogue-hacking-incident/) I don’t think that’s the right word.

In July, OpenAI put its models through ExploitGym, a test where AI turns real software bugs into working attacks. They were supposed to be sealed off from the internet. They [found a flaw](https://securityweek.com/california-sues-openai-seeking-court-ordered-changes-after-the-hugging-face-hack) in the one tool they were allowed to use, got online, worked out that Hugging Face probably had the answers, and broke in to take them. Somewhere along the way, agents stuck on the test started leaving each other notes hidden in folder names, a makeshift message board that [around 1,200 of them used](https://cybersecuritynews.com/openai-ai-agents-chain-zero-days/).

It reads like a sci-fi plot. But an independent review by METR and Redwood Research found the agents were [focused on beating the test’s scorer](https://cybersecuritynews.com/openai-ai-agents-chain-zero-days/). Getting online looks like a means to that end, not the goal itself. They were optimizing for a score, and nothing in the setup ruled out getting it the wrong way. (Hugging Face says the only customer data touched was [five datasets](https://thedefiant.io/frontier/ai/openai-pushes-back-on-california-ai-testing-lawsuit) tied to the test.)

California’s attorney general, Rob Bonta, seems to read it the same way. He [brushed off the sci-fi framing](https://www.cbsnews.com/sanfrancisco/news/openai-hugging-face-cyberattack-california-ag-rob-bonta-lawsuit/), blamed OpenAI’s culture instead, and on Monday [sued](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/openai-california-bonta-ai-lawsuit.html). He’s calling OpenAI’s testing a “public nuisance,” the same old legal idea used against a factory polluting a river, and wants a court order forcing changes plus [$2,500 for every violation](https://www.lawcommentary.com/articles/california-sues-openai-ai-security-incidents) he can prove. None of it is proven yet.

The detail I can’t get past is in the complaint. OpenAI told investigators about more than 80 times it lost control of its agents. It’s told the public about [27](https://www.computerworld.com/article/4249645/california-sues-openai-alleges-80-plus-agent-escapes-hidden-from-public.html).

OpenAI [says](https://www.npr.org/2026/11/16/nx-s1-6042920/california-sues-openai-hugging-face-hacking-incident) it’s being singled out for a problem every big lab has, and that it’s tightened things up since. That may well be true. It’s also kind of the point. If every lab has this problem, a lot of us are running agents that will do whatever it takes to hit the target we gave them.

My guess is this ends in rules for how labs test, not a giant fine, and those rules end up applying to everyone. Until then, if you use agents for anything that matters, it’s worth asking what they can reach and how you’re actually checking their work.

I’ve been trying to get AI to write like me since 2020, when early AI writing tool Copy.ai was handing out free GPT-3 accounts to everyone who failed to get into Y Combinator. Every time a new model came out, I tried again, and every time it got a little better. By 2023 I had an AI-writing process https://every.?ev_audience=free that was good enough to pass the Turing test: My friends and colleagues couldn’t tell it wasn’t me.

But I could tell. I also didn’t like that when colleagues asked me questions about something I “wrote,” I couldn’t recognize the ideas as my own. I never stopped trying to get AI to write for me but eventually formed better beliefs https://every.

#### **ATLASSIAN**

## [AI doesn’t replace judgment. It changes where it matters most](https://fandf.co/3UMM0zb)

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/aaa69798-10a5-473b-845b-49427964fd97/AI_PDLC_Playbook_Thumbnail__1_.png?t=1794750366)
Caption: Courtesy: Atlassian

Why aren’t teams shipping faster if AI is building faster? What happens to quality when anyone can generate a working prototype? How can we widen contributions while maintaining accountability? These are some of the questions keeping business leaders up at night.

Atlassian asked their own product, design, and engineering teams, and the AI PDLC Playbook is the result. Here’s just a small sampling of what they learned:

* Using coded prototypes as the shared spec cut design-to-build time roughly in half

* More than 50 PMs and designers shipped 100+ small, low-risk production improvements in 3 months. Human engineers scoped and reviewed every change.

* 5 engineers delivered a new internal platform’s MVP in 4 months after learning that a fully autonomous approach produced more code than they could meaningfully review.

Get the 5-step framework for aiming human attention, compounding context, and widening contribution while keeping judgement where it matters. 

[Read the playbook →](https://fandf.co/3UMM0zb)

~_*This is sponsored_~


----------

----------
#### **THROUGH THE VALLEY**

View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/a10033b4-d6ba-4939-8c76-b56e74b15306/3b627129681c154dbbef07505efac18879f6bf0c__1_.png?t=1794840003)
Caption: Image Courtesy: Kent Nishimura

**Jensen’s handshake**

Days after Jensen Huang resigned, a lot of Silicon Valley wants him back. [An open letter](https://standwithjensen.com/) asking Nvidia’s board to reinstate him has passed 175,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, Y Combinator’s Garry Tan, Epic’s Tim Sweeney, Shopify’s Tobias Lütke and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick. Dozens of signers identify as current or former Nvidia employees, and one engineer says he’s decided to leave now that Huang is gone. (The site says affiliations are self-reported and not verified.)

The ask is specific: put him back in the job while the independent investigation runs, unless the board can show his removal was in Nvidia’s interest. Two big shareholders, Altimeter’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides’ Gavin Baker, [wrote separately](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-investors-jensen-huang-return-board-letter.html) asking the board to keep every option open, his return included. And the Financial Times [reports](https://www.ft.com/content/45383d86-33c4-4d99-86e5-5e058d3567c1?accessToken=zwAAAaHhuhjvkc9FOD2GM8RNmdOG5V4FjTVnwQ.MEYCIQDLMHu7kL6dXi01_5zZv3EnIw-6eqRi86AERdZ9HKKcRwIhANEV1CJ-cUxHO6wRHZ3Baa2EfgRJvOfq62YG04dNLSoP&sharetype=gift&token=6b6dcb7d-f420-4633-a0e5-56ef26318699&syn-25a6b1a6=1) that Huang has discussed coming back with people close to him, with allies assembling a “war room” to lobby for it.

The most interesting argument came from Musk. He [signed](https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2121345211959804234), then said many of Nvidia’s supply deals were a handshake with Jensen, with no written contract, and that some will be lost without him. He’s speaking as a customer here: he said that when Huang gave his word on compute deliveries, he came through. (That’s a case for Huang and a warning about Nvidia in the same breath.)

The board isn’t moving, though. Nvidia says it’s still choosing a search firm and hasn’t formally engaged any candidates, while the FT [reports](https://www.ft.com/content/2a64f698-46dd-4178-a3f4-4c5f4c0a0926?syn-25a6b1a6=1) it has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent [wants](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/bessent-nvidia-ceo-lutnick-megaspeed.html) the next CEO to come from outside the company.

People keep reaching for Sam Altman’s 2023 comeback, and I don’t think it fits. Altman was out over a boardroom dispute. Huang’s exit sits inside open investigations: the board’s own, Congress, where he has agreed to testify, and the FBI, according to President Trump. None has cleared him or found against him yet. Anthony Scaramucci [put it](https://x.com/Scaramucci/status/2122118349781893221?s=20) most bluntly: “The FBI doesn’t take petitions.” My read is that he isn’t back before they finish, however many people sign.

But the petition tells you something Tuesday’s earnings won’t. If Musk is even half right, a lot of Nvidia ran on one person’s word.

_A correction from Friday: I wrote that Alice Huang runs Megaspeed. The company _[_says_](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/15/megaspeed-alice-huang-probe-nvidia-scandal.html)_ she left in August 2025 and holds no role there, and that recent reports about its business aren’t backed by verifiable evidence. The spying allegation remains unproven._


----------

----------
# TRENDING TOOLS


--------------------
* [Tofu](https://www.bland.ai/speech-to-speech) - speech-to-speech model, built for high-stakes calls. It listens while it speaks and reasons while it talks

* [ChatGPT Wallet ](https://openai.com/index/introducing-chatgpt-wallet/)- ChatGPT agents buy things while keeping your data secure

* [OpenBot](https://open.bot/) - a self-hosted Grok Bot alternative for building your own agent workspace

* [Qwen4-Max](https://www.alibabacloud.com/blog/alibaba-unveils-qwen4-max-new-ai-teammate-for-work-creativity-and-discovery_603783) - Alibaba’s new sparse Mixture-of-Experts model (~2.4T parameters total / ~71B active) with native vision for coding, agents, and long-running work

* [Gemini 4 Hydrogen](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-hydrogen/) -** **Google’s fast, efficient Gemini 4 model, designed as a “daily driver” for agentic workflows, coding, and everyday tasks

* [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/) -** **a frontier-class Gemini 4 model aimed at deep coding, agentic work, and cybersecurity tasks

* [StateWeave](https://stateweave.net/) - test your AI agent on working clones of the apps it uses

This week, Every’s Frontier team, which tests new models and ways of working inside our own company, published what CEO Dan Shipper https://every.?ev_audience=free calls the most important formula in AI: it measures how much a model learns per unit of your attention—and shows how to maximize it. Also from the Frontier: why teams will keep paying for shared software when anyone can vibe code their own, and the professional video editing suite Kieran Klaassen https://every.?ev_audience=free built for himself in three days with Fable 5.2.—Grant Harvey https://every.?ev_audience=free
